newsitem.title: USA: George Wallace threatens to sue over TNT film.
newsitem.headline: George Wallace threatens to sue over TNT film.

text.p: Former Alabama Gov. George Wallace is threatening to sue Turner Network Television over a new made-for-TV movie that he says distorts some of the facts about his stormy political career.

Bedridden and deaf after a quarter-century as a paraplegic, the one-time segregationist told Reuters in an interview last week that he is not angry about the $12 million production, in which he is played by Hollywood actor Gary Sinise. But he has no second thoughts about getting even in court if TNT fails to alter the story line.

"Hollywood is about a lot of junk," the 77-year-old Wallace said while puffing on a cigar in the bedroom of the one-story home where he has lived for the past decade. Despite a host of maladies including Parkinson's disease, Wallace greets visitors with a firm handshake and a steady gaze.
"All these pictures -- dirty pictures and dirty movies," he added in a disgusted tone. "The movie's full of falsehoods and errors. Of course I'm suing."

The movie began filming two weeks ago in Los Angeles and is scheduled to air in August. TNT executives have been receiving many complaints from Wallace's relatives, who are acting on his behalf, about parts of the movie.
After reviewing the film's script, outraged family members sent TNT a four-page memo detailing what they said were historical inaccuracies and distortions.
They have also hired a lawyer, threatened a lawsuit and even sought the advice of Henry Kissinger, who sued the production company run by Ted Turner in a similar dispute.
Wallace's son, George Wallace Jr., has complained that the film depicts his father as an "illiterate, ignorant, corn-pone 'Hee Haw' character."
But the family's main bone of contention is with two scenes depicting incidents they say never happened.

In one, a Wallace aide considers killing Wallace with an ice pick. Later, the same character helps to stop a paralysed Wallace from ending his life by pitching his wheelchair off the porch at the home of another real-life former Alabama governor, James "Big Jim" Folsom.

TNT producers admitted that some of the scenes depicted in the movie never occurred. But they said their intent was to get beyond the Wallace personality in order to present the larger themes of his era, namely racism and redemption.
The movie's producer, Mark Carliner, told Reuters, "There are people speaking for (Wallace). I'm not sure what he really feels."

Wallace's declining health often prevents him from speaking out publicly. In the interview with Reuters, Wallace directed his anger at the film's portrayal of two loyal companions, including his late first wife, Lurleen, who succeeded him as Alabama governor in 1966.
"They made fun of her like she was a redneck. She was governor of the state when she died (of cancer)," he said.
Wallace and others have said they believe the character who plots his murder in the film was based on longtime aide Eddie Holcey, who has assisted the former governor since 1973.
"He's loyal. And he's been with me a long time," Wallace said.

First elected governor of Alabama in 1962, Wallace drew national attention by proclaiming "segregation forever" in his inaugural address. But it was his televised stand in "the schoolhouse door" against integration at the University of Alabama that immortalised him as an infamous symbol of the Civil Rights era.

After being paralysed from the waist down by an assassination attempt during his 1972 presidential campaign, he renounced segregation and has struggled over the past 25 years to redeem his image by championing the cause of racial reconciliation.
